newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia's LPG prices fall from 10-year high.
newsitem.headline: Asia's LPG prices fall from 10-year high.

text.p: The price of liquefied petroleum gas, used for home heating, cooking and petrochemicals, is slipping from a 10-year high in Asia as demand falls and temperatures rise, sources said on Tuesday.
Globally, strong demand in Europe was supporting prices, sucking in stocks from outside the region.

But in Asia, demand from China -- the key to the region's demand and supply balance -- has dropped sharply after it built up stocks ahead of the Chinese New Year. A moderate winter in northern Asia had limited demand from elsewhere, traders said.
Chinese New Year starts on February 7.
"Most industries will be closed during the period (and) demand for LPG for petrochemical feedstocks will fall drastically," said an LPG trader in China.
LPG prices soared last year largely on growing demand for the versatile product and cold weather in all major consuming centres. Rising crude and product prices helped.

Earlier this month Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest exporter of LPG, set a Contract Price (CP) of $330 per tonne of propane and butane, more than $100 higher than a year ago and a 10-year high. The CP is used as the LPG market's price benchmark.
But prices in Asia have not kept pace. While using the CP as the base for price negotiations, premiums have been falling.
Premiums over the CP for free-on-board (FOB) south China fell this week to $65-$75 per tonne from $75-79 last week.
Prices were lower in northerly Shanghai, at $60-$70 per tonne premium, down from $72-$75 last week.
Traders said there were at least three floating storage vessels of around 40,000 tonnes each anchored off southern China, two near Shanghai and one other off Kaohsiung in Taiwan.
They said supplies from the floating storage would be more than sufficient to meet Chinese demand during the festive season. China normally consumes 250,000 to 330,000 tonnes of LPG per month.

In north Asia, a mild winter and Saudi Arabia's high CP price were keeping potential buyers sidelined. Major importer Japan was expecting normal temperatures through February and March, weather forecasters said.
"We are very reluctant to buy spot supplies, the CP at $330 is just incredibly high. We would lose money if we sell in the retail market" said a Japanese trader.

LPG delivered to Japan was assessed around $30 per tonne premium, down from $35-$40 last week, despite rising freight costs. Freight between Saudi Arabia and North Asia on single port to single port basis was currently $30-$32 per tonne, up from $25-$28 early last week.
Demand from state-owned Indian Oil Corp, which has tendered to buy 142-145,000 tonnes of butane for March 1-21 delivery, would do little to tighten supply, traders said.
Abu Dhabi and Kuwait each have unsold spot cargoes of 40,000 tonnes each for end February loading.
Malaysia was offering up to 4,000 tonnes for sale in February, and Thailand had supplies, traders said.
These would weigh on the market, which is mostly fed through long-term contracts.
